source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: Theory: mapping is chosen by three soft constraints at once (structure/isomorphism, semantic similarity, pragmatic centrality). ACME settles by parallel constraint satisfaction.
numbers: ACME typically settles in well under 100 update cycles; never more than 220 cycles in any reported run. Convergence-problem mapping settled by cycle 31 for the laser/fragile-glass version.
quote: A theory of analogical mapping based upon interacting structural, semantic, and pragmatic constraints
limits: Simulations only. No new human data in this paper. Pragmatic input is set by the modeller by hand (weights), not derived.
agent_relevance: Choosing among candidate mappings is a weighted trade-off, not a rule. Our agent can score each candidate mapping on structure, meaning-match and goal-fit and pick the best joint score.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: ACME reproduces the ranking of human difficulty for story-analogy versions: semantic similarity helps, but systematicity only matters when similarity misleads (cross-mapped).
numbers: Jealous Animals stories, six versions. Cycles to success rose slightly from similar/similar to different versions, then sharply in the cross-mapped S/D version. In the UNSYSTEMATIC cross-mapped version ACME failed to settle on the correct mapping. It succeeded if inhibition was lowered from -.2 to -.1 or min raised from -1 to -.3.
limits: Result is parameter sensitive. Fit is qualitative (cycles to success vs human accuracy), not a quantitative fit.
agent_relevance: A misleading surface match can beat true structure when structure is weak. Guard: when similarity and structure disagree, require strong structural evidence before overriding surface match.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: ACME was run on convergence-problem analogies (radiation problem vs lightbulb and general stories) and reproduced the ordering of human transfer rates from Holyoak and Koh (1987).
numbers: Four lightbulb-problem versions; cycles-to-success used as a difficulty proxy; Holyoak and Koh measured percent of undergraduates giving the convergence solution before and after a hint.
limits: Comparison is ordinal. The exact human percentages were not extracted this session.
agent_relevance: Same structure, different surface: mapping can be found, retrieval is the harder step (see 05_analogical_retrieval).

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: ACME handles formally isomorphic analogs with no shared predicates, and also non-isomorphic cases (politics, Socrates as midwife), by keeping one-to-one pressure soft.
numbers: Settling times in the paper: 59-60 cycles for a bare formal isomorphism, 71-72 for the minimalist problem, 83-105 for Socrates-midwife variants, 402 cycles for one large network.
limits: One-to-one is only a soft inhibition, so many-to-one mappings are allowed. Large networks settle slowly.
agent_relevance: The agent should not enforce one-to-one hard. Allow a ranked list with ties flagged.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 1: the reasoner's goal changed which of two structurally ambiguous mappings people chose.
numbers: Ambiguous country Anthar mapped to prosperous Grandus by 54% vs poor Minutus by 19% in the Trade goal; reversed in Membership goal (21% vs 58%). chi2(1,N=53)=11.78, p<.001. Winter country mapped to Grandus by 31% (Trade) vs 4% (Membership), chi2(2,N=55)=6.82, p<.05.
quote: processing goals can serve to guide analogical mapping
limits: Undergraduates; long science-fiction stories; 12 participants dropped for misunderstanding. Many mappings are left blank or partial.
agent_relevance: Mapping preference depends on the stated purpose. Our agent should state the goal before mapping and re-map if the goal changes.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 2: goal effect holds whether the goal stresses a relation (military vs economic) or an object (Millpower vs Hungerall). Goal-irrelevant info still leaks in as many-to-one mappings.
numbers: N=159 kept of 165 (6 dropped). Control condition: 71% gave the same economic recommendation for Hungerall as for Barebrute, and 82% the same military one for Millpower. Military condition: 77% vs 13%. In the 2-to-1 direction control, 8 of 16 (50%) mapped both Hungerall and Millpower to Barebrute; 32% did so even when the goal favoured one.
limits: Unambiguous countries (Afflu, Compak) were mapped as expected by about 90% in every condition, so the goal only acts where structure is ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Goal acts as a tie-breaker, not an override. Good design: apply goal weighting only to the ambiguous part of a mapping.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 3: with a goal-relevant relation (Professional vs Romantic subplot) and an incidental relation (Inheritance), mapping used both; plot extension used only the goal-relevant one.
numbers: Plot-extension: 97% of those who wrote an analogous story used the goal-appropriate theme, chi2(1,N=107)=95.33. Mapping task: goal-relevant mapping 72% vs 28%, chi2=16.41; incidental-relation mapping 65% vs 35%, chi2(1,N=88)=7.68, p<.01. 23 people followed the goal in plot-extension but not mapping vs 1 the reverse.
quote: goal-irrelevant information contributed to many-to-one mappings
limits: Only 69% of participants gave usable congruent answers. Same lab as the theory (self-test risk); no outside replication found in this session.
agent_relevance: Supports a soft goal filter (attenuation), not a hard one: irrelevant relations still push the mapping. Do not strip all goal-irrelevant info before mapping.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: ACME with goals modelled as inhibitory selective attention reproduced the qualitative pattern of all three experiments.
numbers: Simulated Experiments 1, 2 and 3 (and the earlier 3* variant); fit judged by matching percentage patterns, not by a fit statistic.
limits: Free parameters chosen by the modellers. Qualitative match only.
agent_relevance: Goal as attention weights on propositions is a cheap, implementable device: scale how much each source fact counts.

source: Spellman & Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: Boundary condition: goals alter mapping only for elements ambiguous on structure; unambiguous elements are stable.
numbers: Afflu to Grainwell and Compak to Mightless mapped by about 90% in all five goal conditions (Exp 2).
limits: UCLA undergraduates only; no cultural or expertise comparison.
agent_relevance: Do not let goal override firm structural matches.

source: Krawczyk, Holyoak & Hummel (2004) Structural constraints and object similarity in analogical mapping and inference
finding: Discriminating experiment against SME: when object similarity and relational structure compete under high relational complexity, people weight them about equally in mapping and inference.
numbers: N=48 UCLA students. Mapping type means (proportion of mappings): Object-similar 0.33, Relational 0.30, Sensible-other 0.32, Unrelated 0.06; F(3,141)=21.64, p<.01. Inferences: Object 0.28, Relational 0.23, Sensible-other 0.50, Unrelated 0.02; F(3,141)=18.78. Mean 2.36 mappings per character.
quote: equal importance for relational structure and object similarity
limits: Single story pair with a cheating-employee relation. Quiz accuracy was .74 before correction, so comprehension was imperfect.
agent_relevance: Directly refutes 'structure always wins'. Object-level match deserves real weight when relational load is high.

source: Krawczyk, Holyoak & Hummel (2004) Structural constraints and object similarity in analogical mapping and inference
finding: SME (structure-pre-eminent) scored the relational inference far above the object-similarity inference; LISA with soft constraints and limited working memory reproduced the human mixture.
numbers: SME structural evaluation: object inference 1.01 vs relational inference 6.21 (run once, deterministic). LISA runs: object-based inference 24%, relational 18%, mixtures 48%.
limits: Model comparison on one item set. SME has been extended since; this tests one version. Markman ran the SME simulations.
agent_relevance: A stochastic or multi-sample mapping is closer to people than a single deterministic best match; sample several mappings and compare.

source: Krawczyk, Holyoak & Hummel (2004) Structural constraints and object similarity in analogical mapping and inference
finding: Complexity moderates the weight of structure: under high relational load object similarity gets as much weight as relations. Earlier lower-load work found structure dominating.
numbers: Same N=48 experiment; earlier studies (Gentner, Markman) used lower-load items.
limits: Moderator is inferred from comparison with earlier studies, not manipulated within this study.
agent_relevance: When many relations must be held at once, expect the model to lean on surface cues; reduce load by chunking the mapping into small sub-maps.

source: Krawczyk, Holyoak & Hummel (2004) Structural constraints and object similarity in analogical mapping and inference
finding: Many-mapping behaviour is common: people report multiple mappings per element under complexity (also Spellman and Holyoak 1992, 1996; Markman).
numbers: Mean 2.36 mappings per character in KH04; 50% many-to-one in SH96 control.
limits: Reporting format allowed multiple answers, which invites it.
agent_relevance: Do not force a single mapping early; keep 2-3 candidates when scores are close, and test them with a downstream check.

source: Lu, Ichien & Holyoak (2022) Probabilistic analogical mapping with semantic relation networks
finding: Probabilistic analogical mapping (PAM), a successor of multiconstraint ideas using word vectors and learned relation vectors, nearly matches human mapping accuracy on 20 keyword analogies.
numbers: PAM mean accuracy 85% vs adult humans 88% (Turney 2008); Turney's LRME model 92%. Science analogies 0.79 (humans 0.85); metaphors 0.90 (humans 0.91). Without edge/relation similarity: 77%; with word2vec-diff instead of BART relation vectors: 77%.
limits: PAM beat humans on 10 problems, lost on 9, tied on 1. Relation vectors came from BART trained on other data; keyword-level analogs only.
agent_relevance: Relation similarity adds about 8 points over node similarity alone. Our agent should compare relations, not only the objects.

source: Lu, Ichien & Holyoak (2022) Probabilistic analogical mapping with semantic relation networks
finding: PAM simulates the Spellman and Holyoak 1996 Experiment 2 goal effect by raising attention weights on goal-relevant relations; control gives equal probability to both mappings.
numbers: Attention weight sampled uniformly from [1,1.1], averaged over 1000 samples per condition; node similarity could not discriminate (same vector for all countries).
limits: PAM has no explicit decision rule for ambiguous cases; the paper notes about half of human controls gave both mappings.
agent_relevance: A small weight (up to 10%) on goal-relevant relations is enough to flip a tie. Cheap lever for the agent.

source: Lu, Ichien & Holyoak (2022) Probabilistic analogical mapping with semantic relation networks
finding: Retrieval and mapping dissociate: Keane (1987) found same-domain sources retrieved far more than remote ones, but once cued, solving was equally high.
numbers: Keane 1987 Exp 1: 88% retrieved the same-domain (surgeon) story vs 12% the remote (general-fortress) story; convergence solution about 86% either way once the source was cued.
limits: Reported secondhand through the PAM paper, which I opened; not the original.
agent_relevance: Mapping is not the bottleneck; retrieval is. Spend effort on getting the right source into context, then map.

source: Spellman, Holyoak & Morrison (2001) Analogical priming via semantic relations
finding: Relational priming appears only when people are told to note and use the relation, consistent with relations being used strategically, not automatically.
numbers: Exp 1C (note and use relation): intact primes 761 ms vs split primes 786 ms, a 25 ms effect, F(1,23)=36.54, p<.0001. Merely reading primes gave no effect.
quote: relational priming was observed under instructions to note and use the semantic relations
limits: Lexical decision, 24 participants in 1C. Small effect in ms.
agent_relevance: Relation use needs an explicit instruction. In prompts, tell the model which relation to track.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat undergraduates on text matrix, letter-string and verbal analogies, but was worse than people on story analogies requiring higher-order causal mapping.
numbers: Digit matrices (human N=40): GPT-3 above humans, OR=1.88, p=0.005. Letter strings (N=57): GPT-3 above humans on zero-generalization, OR=1.76, p=0.0007. Story analogies (N=54): GPT-3 below humans, OR=0.37, p=0.0003; 15 of 54 people chose the analogous story every trial. GPT-4 preliminary: better on stories.
quote: GPT-3 displayed a surprisingly strong capacity for abstract pattern induction
limits: Later work (Lewis and Mitchell) shows the success is brittle. Possible training-data contamination for letter-string and verbal items. Humans are UCLA undergraduates or MTurk workers.
agent_relevance: Higher-order relational mapping across stories is where LLMs were weakest; use explicit structure checks there.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 showed human-like sensitivity to semantic distance and to causal (higher-order) relations.
numbers: Jones et al. verbal analogies: semantic distance effect for GPT-3 OR=3.24, p=0.0165. Story analogies: both GPT-3 and humans chose the shared-causal-relations story above chance (humans combined t(53)=21.3; far condition t(53)=16.7).
limits: Statistical sensitivity does not prove the mechanism is mapping.
agent_relevance: Models may show the right soft-constraint effects. Still test with surface-distractor variants.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Counterfactual letter-string analogies (permuted or symbol alphabets) cut GPT accuracy sharply while humans stayed high.
numbers: Human data 1,876 samples; GPT models 6,840 each; GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 (gpt-4-turbo-0613) at temperature 0. Overall human accuracy 0.753 [0.734, 0.773] in Table 2 (as extracted).
quote: the GPT models' performance declines sharply on the counterfactual set
limits: Prolific humans; prompts tuned from Hodel and West. Letter strings are a narrow domain. Humans here scored higher than Webb's humans.
agent_relevance: Passing a standard item is not proof of structure use. Test mapping on a counterfactual rewording (schema G3: pass on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Failed generalisation of the Webb result: the models understood the new letter order, so the drop is not a simple misunderstanding.
numbers: Counterfactual comprehension check: GPT-4 close to 1.00 on successor and predecessor for permuted-alphabet letters in the cells read; GPT-3 successor 0.82 on one unpermuted cell.
limits: Cell-level numbers come from a messy text extraction; trust the direction, not the exact cells.
agent_relevance: Good example of a pass that was fitted to training-like items (guardrail G3).

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024/25) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-4 story-analogy accuracy is biased by answer order and drops under paraphrase; humans show no order bias.
numbers: 18 far-analogy story problems. GPT-4 correct answer first 0.89 (16/18), second 0.61 (11/18), total 0.75 (27/36). Humans (N=245, 6 problems each): first 0.78 (292/373), second 0.78 (272/347), total 0.78 (564/720). Paraphrased correct story: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (31/36 to 26/36); humans 0.78 to 0.70 (564/720 to 503/720).
limits: Only 18 stories, so the paraphrase gap is not tested for significance by the authors. Both groups drop, suggesting sentence-level surface overlap helped both.
agent_relevance: Always randomise answer order and run both orders; treat order disagreement as a failed check.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024/25) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Digit matrices: GPT performance drops on one of two variants but not the other. Letter-string error types differ: LLMs apply a wrong rule, humans more often find a valid alternate rule.
numbers: Two matrix variants: random blank position and non-numeric symbols. Error types: alternate-rule GPT-3 5.81%, GPT-4 22.00%, humans 38.59%; incorrect-rule GPT-3 55.48%, GPT-4 42.67%, humans 34.24%.
limits: Error categories hand coded. Exact matrix accuracies not extracted. Which variant hurt is not stated in the text I read.
agent_relevance: LLM failures are wrong-rule failures. Ask for the rule first, then apply it.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas & Mitchell (2024/25) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Children and adults carry letter-string analogy skill across alphabets unchanged; four LLMs lose accuracy as the domain gets less familiar.
numbers: Mean proportion correct (Latin/Greek/Symbol). Adults (n=62) .88/.91/.89. Children 7-9 y (n=41) .62/.66/.67. GPT-4o .85/.63/.48. Claude-3.5 .68/.62/.46. Llama-3.1 405B .79/.74/.27. Gemma-2 27B .60/.39/.14. LLM alphabet effect p<.001 for all four; humans p=1.0.
limits: Five items per alphabet, 54 runs per LLM. Predecessor/successor knowledge check explained the failure only in part.
agent_relevance: Transfer to far domains is where the LLM falls behind even 8-year-olds. Keep far-transfer mapping behind an explicit structure table.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas & Mitchell (2024/25) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Hardest rules for both children and LLMs: the predecessor rule and the second-successor rule.
numbers: Item 5 (predecessor plus repeat): adults .81, children .38, GPT-4o .39, Claude-3.5 .20. Item 3 (second successor): adults .82, children .52, GPT-4o .45.
limits: Few items; rule difficulty is confounded with item.
agent_relevance: Report per-rule accuracy, not just totals.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting (the model recalls its own related problems before solving) beats 0-shot and few-shot chain of thought on average.
numbers: Average accuracy gain +4% over baselines across GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003, PaLM 2. K=5 self-generated exemplars for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench. GSM8K 5-shot CoT 75.0% vs 75.8-77.8% for the self-generated variants (column mapping uncertain in extraction).
limits: GSM8K gain is small, MATH and code larger. Generated knowledge helped only on the hardest task (Codeforces). This is analogical retrieval, not constraint-based mapping; the model's pick of 'relevant' problems is unchecked.
agent_relevance: A cheap addition with modest gain. The paper does not test choosing among competing mappings.

source: Ichien, Stamenkovic & Holyoak (2023) LLM displays emergent ability to interpret novel literary metaphors
finding: GPT-4 interprets figurative language pragmatically like people, including restoring the canonical meaning of reversed metaphors.
numbers: Fig-QA 1,146 test metaphors: humans 94.42%, GPT-3 Davinci zero-shot 68.41%, fine-tuned RoBERTa 90.32%, GPT-4 zero-shot 91.27%. Reversed metaphors: GPT-4 restored canonical meaning 56% vs humans 50%; point-biserial r=0.79 across 55 metaphors, p<.001.
quote: GPT-4 resembles humans in its sensitivity to pragmatic constraints on communication
limits: Metaphor interpretation, not explicit mapping. 3.35% of GPT-4 answers refused both options and were counted wrong.
agent_relevance: LLMs follow pragmatic (Gricean) constraints in interpretation. Supports using purpose as a prompt input.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere & Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Semantic structure and content mapping tasks: advanced LLMs match humans in several conditions but differ under semantic distractors; condition effects differ between humans and models.
numbers: Compared GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama-405B and older models with humans. Subject-type by condition interaction significant: GPT-4 vs humans chi2(7)=115.19, p<0.001; Claude 3 vs humans chi2(7)=173.65; Claude coefficient -0.8706, z=-5.608. A Distracted condition tested semantic distractors.
limits: Exact accuracies are in figures not extracted. Authors say LLMs give a how-possibly, not how-actually, explanation.
agent_relevance: LLM sensitivity to distractors differs from humans; add a distractor check in mapping.

source: Petersen, Stevenson & van der Plas (2025) Modelling analogies and analogical reasoning: connecting cognitive science theory and NLP research
finding: Survey ties NLP analogy work to Gentner and Holyoak theory and notes that pragmatic centrality (goal) is the least handled constraint in NLP models.
numbers: Theoretical survey. States mapping depends on purpose and that which entities enter the mapping can change with the objective.
quote: Analogical reasoning and MAPPING always take place in the context of an overarching goal
limits: No new data; a survey of what is missing, not of measured effects.
agent_relevance: Flags the gap our agent can fill by passing the goal explicitly to the mapping step.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) Why do we need neuro-symbolic AI to model pragmatic analogies?
finding: Argues LLMs struggle most on pragmatic analogies (those needing outside knowledge and goals) and proposes neuro-symbolic help to guide mapping.
numbers: Four levels: lexical, syntactic, semantic, pragmatic analogies. No quantitative results reported in the parts read.
limits: Position article; weak evidence. Only the abstract and introduction were read in detail.
agent_relevance: Treat as a design hint, not a result.
